issues.legal_issue: A court assessing the credibility of witnesses who testify to a will’s execution may consider the surrounding circumstances and probabilities, rather than examining their testimony in isolation.
material_facts: The dispute concerned whether a purported will had been executed by the deceased and duly attested.
The court assessed the testimony of the alleged attesting witnesses and the scribe alongside circumstances concerning the document and its execution.
issues.conclusion: The court held that credibility may be assessed in light of surrounding circumstances and probabilities, including circumstances emerging from the evidence or the document itself.
issues.legal_principle: Witness credibility is not determined only by the manner of testimony or demeanour; the court may consider surrounding circumstances and probabilities to assess trustworthiness. Evidence of execution should not be lightly rejected on mere speculation, but it is not to be considered independently of attendant circumstances. The court relied on Kristo Gopal v. Baidya Nath and Chotey Narain Singh v. Mt. Ratan Koer, and referred to the prudent-mind approach in H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B. N. Thimmajamma.

predicates.will_execution_dispute: A court is deciding whether witnesses truthfully testified to the execution of a will.
predicates.surrounding_circumstances_available: Evidence or the document itself provides circumstances relevant to whether the witnesses’ testimony is trustworthy.

issues.definition: When a will’s execution is disputed and relevant surrounding circumstances are available, witness credibility is assessed in light of those circumstances.

issues.legal_issue: A person propounding a will must remove legitimate suspicions about its genuineness before the court accepts it as the testator’s will.
material_facts: The purported will gave almost the entire estate to a distant relative and made limited provision for the testator’s widow and daughters.
The beneficiary had an active role in procuring the document, which was prepared at his home with a scribe and witnesses connected to him.
The court identified several circumstances raising suspicion about the document and its execution, and found no evidence that satisfactorily removed those suspicions.
issues.conclusion: The court held that the propounder had to satisfy the court about the will’s genuineness by removing the suspicions naturally arising from the circumstances, and that this burden had not been met.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, the special requirement of attestation applies to proof of a will. The propounder bears the onus of proving the will; absent suspicious circumstances, proof of testamentary capacity and the testator’s legally required signature, together with due attestation, may discharge that onus. If suspicious circumstances arise, the propounder must explain them to the court’s satisfaction; a benefit to a propounder who actively participated in execution is a relevant suspicion. Where fraud, coercion, or undue influence is alleged, the person alleging it bears the burden of proving it. The court relied on Sarat Kumari Bibi v. Sakhi Chand, H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B. N. Thimmajamma, Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, and Tyrrell v. Painton.

predicates.will_propounded: A person asks a court to accept a document as a testator’s will.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_present: Circumstances surrounding the document, its execution, or its dispositions give the court legitimate reason to doubt that it represents the testator’s free and genuine act.

issues.definition: When a person propounds a will and legitimate suspicions arise, the propounder must remove those suspicions to obtain acceptance of the will.

issues.legal_issue: A purported will is not established as genuine where the circumstances of its execution and contents raise substantial suspicions and the propounder does not satisfactorily remove them.
material_facts: The purported will was said to have been executed at the beneficiary’s home, although the testator had been at a distant village until the previous afternoon and execution at the stated time was highly improbable.
The scribe and attesting witnesses were connected to the beneficiary rather than being shown to be the testator’s own friends; the beneficiary had actively participated in procuring the document.
The document was on flimsy paper, used high-flown Urdu although the testator could not read or write Urdu, and its layout suggested that the testator’s signature may have preceded the writing.
The document gave almost the entire substantial estate to a distant relative while providing little for the testator’s widow and daughters, despite the testator continuing to live with his wife.
The beneficiary did not establish that the will was brought to light promptly after the testator’s death, and the widow continued to possess the cash, valuables, and other movables.
The court found no satisfactory evidence removing the suspicions arising from these circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The court upheld the finding that the purported will was not genuine, rejected the evidence offered to prove its execution, and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The propounder must prove execution and attestation and, where suspicious circumstances arise, remove them to the court’s satisfaction. The court may assess the credibility of execution witnesses against all attendant circumstances and the contents of the document. The court applied the principles in section 63 of the Indian Succession Act and relied on Sarat Kumari Bibi v. Sakhi Chand, H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B. N. Thimmajamma, Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, Kristo Gopal v. Baidya Nath, Chotey Narain Singh v. Mt. Ratan Koer, and Tyrrell v. Painton.

rule.if: appeal_over_will_genuineness and execution_timing_improbable and beneficiary_connected_execution and witnesses_connected_to_beneficiary and suspicious_document_features and dispositions_exclude_close_family and delayed_or_inconsistent_claim and not suspicions_satisfactorily_explained

predicates.appeal_over_will_genuineness: An appeal challenges a decision about whether a purported will is genuine.
predicates.execution_timing_improbable: The circumstances make it highly improbable that the testator could have reached the stated place and executed the will at the stated time.
predicates.beneficiary_connected_execution: The purported will was prepared at a beneficiary’s home and the beneficiary actively participated in procuring its execution.
predicates.witnesses_connected_to_beneficiary: The scribe or attesting witnesses were connected to the beneficiary rather than shown to be the testator’s own associates.
predicates.suspicious_document_features: The paper, language, layout, or signature on the document gives reason to doubt that it was prepared and signed as represented.
predicates.dispositions_exclude_close_family: The document gives most of the estate to a distant beneficiary while making little provision for close family members.
predicates.delayed_or_inconsistent_claim: The beneficiary did not establish prompt disclosure of the will and the testator’s property remained in another person’s possession in a manner inconsistent with the beneficiary’s asserted claim.
predicates.suspicion_satisfactorily_explained: The propounder provided evidence that satisfactorily dispelled the suspicions arising from the circumstances.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a will’s genuineness, the execution circumstances, beneficiary connections, document features, dispositions, and subsequent conduct raise suspicions, and those suspicions are not satisfactorily explained, the will is rejected as not genuine.
